analysis.one_liner: Requires electronics makers to sell repair parts, tools, and manuals to owners and independent repair shops.
analysis.headline: The Fair Repair Act was introduced in February 2026 with a Democratic sponsor and two cosponsors, and has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since the day it was introduced.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies that make digital electronics — phones, laptops, appliances, and similar products — to sell or provide documentation, parts, and repair tools to device owners and independent repair shops on the same terms they give their own authorized repair network. It would also ban "parts pairing," the software practice that makes a device work worse or refuse to function when someone installs a non-manufacturer part. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could enforce these rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who owns or leases a digital device: people who want to fix a phone or laptop themselves, take it to a neighborhood repair shop, or keep using an older product instead of replacing it. Independent repair businesses gain access to the same parts, tools, and manuals that factory-authorized shops get. Farmers, small businesses, and school IT departments that repair their own equipment would no longer face software locks that force a trip to the manufacturer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Device owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must make documentation, parts, and tools — including software updates — available to owners and independent repair providers on terms no worse than those given to their own authorized shops [S2].

The bill bans parts pairing and similar mechanisms that would stop a working replacement part from functioning, reduce a device's performance after an independent repair, trigger false warnings, raise future repair prices, or restrict who can buy parts [S2].
It requires manufacturers to provide the special tools needed to disable and reset security locks during repair, so a locked device can still be fixed [S2].
The FTC can enforce violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue for injunctions, civil penalties, restitution, and damages on behalf of residents [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Original equipment manufacturers of digital electronics — companies that sell phones, computers, and other devices — bear the cost of releasing documentation, selling parts at their best authorized-shop terms, and giving up parts-pairing controls. The bill does not apply to motor vehicles, medical devices, off-road vehicles (aircraft, motorcycles, boats, ATVs), or emergency-communications equipment [S2].

drawbacks.text: The bill limits manufacturer liability: an OEM is not liable for damage, data loss, or privacy breaches that occur during a repair done by an independent shop or owner, and does not have to warrant independent repairs [S2]. An honest supporter would acknowledge this shifts repair risks onto consumers.

The bill carves out whole sectors: motor vehicles, medical devices, off-road and non-road vehicles, and safety communications equipment are all excluded, so farmers' tractors, hospital equipment, and motorcycles are not covered by this bill [S2].

Manufacturers keep a trade-secret carve-out — they need not divulge trade secrets except as necessary to provide parts, tools, and documentation — which critics could argue leaves room to withhold information [S2].

Some manufacturers and security researchers have argued that broadly mandating access to diagnostic software and security-lock bypass tools raises cybersecurity and safety risks; the bill responds with trade-secret and liability provisions rather than technical restrictions [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — letting people repair what they own at a fair price instead of being pushed toward manufacturer-only service or replacement — is real and would save consumers money and reduce electronic waste. The costs are narrower than critics claim, because manufacturers can still protect genuine trade secrets and are shielded from liability for independent repairs. The bill's biggest design weakness is what it leaves out: the exclusions for vehicles, medical devices, and farm-adjacent equipment remove many of the situations where repair restrictions cost people the most, such as tractors. As written, it is a solid but partial right-to-repair law.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — has been taken since.

narrative.text: Representative Joseph Morelle introduced the Fair Repair Act on February 5, 2026, joined by Representative Perez, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1] [S4].
The bill has two cosponsors, both Democrats [S3].
Since the referral, the bill's only entry in its action history is the introduction and committee referral on February 5, 2026 [S4].
The 119th Congress is still in session, so the bill could still receive committee action before January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electronics manufacturers keep the status quo for now: with no committee action, no vote, and only two cosponsors, their repair restrictions remain in place while the bill sits. Consumers keep paying manufacturer-linked repair prices.

for.name: Rep. Joseph Morelle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Repair Act on February 5, 2026 and referred it to Energy and Commerce.

for.name: Rep. Perez
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction as one of its two cosponsors.

for.name: Independent repair industry and right-to-repair advocates
for.what_they_did: Long-running national campaign for right-to-repair laws at the state and federal level, which this bill follows.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on February 5, 2026; no hearing, markup, or floor action has been scheduled.

against.name: Electronics manufacturers
against.role: Manufacturers of phones, computers, and digital devices
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed right-to-repair legislation and lobbied against similar state bills, since parts pairing and authorized-repair networks are part of their service business model.

sides.party_line_note: Both cosponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on; right-to-repair has drawn some bipartisan interest nationally, but this bill's list is all-Democratic so far [S3].

industries.industry: Consumer electronics manufacturers (phones, laptops, and other digital devices)
industries.note: The bill would end their exclusive control over repair by forcing them to sell parts, tools, and manuals at their best authorized-shop terms and to stop using parts pairing to degrade non-factory repairs. Their interest in keeping repair pricing and service inside their own network runs against device owners who want cheaper repair options.
They would get the same documentation, parts, and tools as factory-authorized shops, letting them compete on repair services they are currently locked out of or restricted from performing.

industries.industry: Motor vehicle, medical device, and off-road vehicle makers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempts them, so their repair restrictions are untouched; they gained relative to the electronics sector by being left out entirely.

industries.industry: Device owners and the secondhand/refurbishment market
industries.note: Repairability extends the usable life of phones, laptops, and appliances, cutting replacement costs and supporting resale and refurbishment businesses.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has no action beyond referral, only two cosponsors, and no bipartisan sign-on, which is where most right-to-repair bills in Congress have stalled: they rarely get a hearing in Energy and Commerce unless leadership prioritizes them. Barring a surge of cosponsors or a committee push, it will likely die quietly at the end of the 119th Congress in January 2027.
